overview.title: Plotting every channel of every activation
overview.main_topic: Interpreting the sixth first-layer channel, then listing 10.6, which tiles all channels of all nine activations into one normalized grid per layer
overview.central_idea: Channel 6 of the first layer looks like a diagonal edge detector, but learned filters vary from run to run. To see everything at once, listing 10.6 loops over the nine activations. For each one it standardizes every channel to the 0–255 display range, places the channels into a grid 16 channels wide with 1-pixel separators, and shows the grid with `imshow`.
overview.importance: This listing produces figure 10.3 (p.314), the chapter's main evidence that convnet representations become more abstract and sparser with depth. The per-channel normalization trick is a standard pattern for displaying activations whose raw scales differ widely.
learning_objectives: Explain why individual learned filters are not reproducible across training runs
Trace how listing 10.6 computes the grid dimensions from size and n_features
Understand the per-channel standardization `(x - mean)/std * 64 + 128` followed by clipping to [0, 255]
Explain why all-zero channels are skipped during normalization
Map channel_index to its position in the display grid

summary:
The page opens by interpreting figure 10.2 (p.312): the sixth channel of the first layer **appears to encode a diagonal edge detector**. The authors add a caveat: your own channels may look different, because **the specific filters learned by convolution layers aren't deterministic**. Random initialization and stochastic training produce a different set of filters, in a different order, each time.

They then move from one channel to all of them: "a complete visualization of all the activations in the network" (figure 10.3, p.314). Every channel of each of the nine layer activations is extracted and plotted, and for each layer the channels are stacked side by side in one big grid.

**Listing 10.6** does this:

- `images_per_row = 16` fixes the grid width at 16 channels.
- It iterates over `zip(layer_names, activations)`, so each grid gets its layer's name as a title.
- For each activation, of shape `(1, size, size, n_features)`, it reads `n_features` (channels) and `size` (spatial side), computes `n_cols = n_features // 16` and allocates an empty `display_grid` with a 1-pixel gap between tiles.
- For each channel it copies the 2D map. If the map is not all zero, it standardizes it (subtract mean, divide by std), then scales by 64 and shifts by 128. Finally it clips to [0, 255] and casts to `uint8`. The callout states that this normalizes channel values within [0, 255] and that **all-zero channels are kept at zero**.
- It writes the tile into its slot of the grid.
- It creates a figure sized proportionally to the grid (`scale = 1.0 / size`), sets the title to the layer name, turns off grid lines and axes, and shows the grid with `imshow(..., cmap="viridis")`.

The output is nine large images, one per layer, which together form figure 10.3. The authors' observations about them (edge detectors, rising abstraction, rising sparsity) follow on p.314.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The channel plotted in figure 10.2 seems to be a diagonal edge detector. Readers' channels may differ, because the filters a convolution layer learns are not deterministic.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In figure 10.2 the bright responses lie along edges of one orientation, such as the outline of the ear. That is the signature of a filter tuned to intensity changes in that direction. Which filter ends up at index 5, and exactly what it detects, depends on random weight initialization, the random order of training batches, data augmentation randomness and non-deterministic GPU operations. Another run will learn a similar family of filters (edges, colors, textures), but their order and details will differ.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It warns readers not to expect a pixel-perfect match with the book. It also makes a deeper point: the individual index of a unit has no fixed meaning, and only the population of learned features is reproducible in a statistical sense.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Permutation symmetry: swapping two filters in a layer (and the corresponding input weights of the next layer) yields an identical function, so nothing makes 'channel 5' special.

terminology.meaning: A filter whose response is large where image intensity changes sharply along a particular direction.
Producing the same result on every run; training with random initialization is not.

p.314: the first layer as a whole acts as a collection of various edge detectors

concepts.name: Non-determinism of learned filters
concepts.definition: Different training runs of the same architecture learn different specific filters, in different orders.
concepts.intuition: There are many equally good sets of filters, and randomness decides which one you end up with.
concepts.technical: Sources include random initialization, random shuffling and augmentation, and non-deterministic GPU kernels. Permutation symmetry of units means channel indices carry no inherent meaning.
concepts.significance: Explains why the reader's channel 5 may not match figure 10.2.
concepts.example: In your run the diagonal-edge filter might be channel 17, and channel 5 might respond to a color.
concepts.misconception: Non-determinism does not mean the learned features are arbitrary. Early layers reliably learn edge- and color-like detectors.

concepts.name: Per-channel normalization for display
concepts.definition: Rescaling each channel independently so its values fill a common display range, here via standardization, ×64, +128 and clipping to [0, 255].
concepts.intuition: Each channel is given its own contrast setting so faint and strong channels are both visible.
concepts.technical: $x' = \operatorname{clip}(64\,(x-\mu)/\sigma + 128,\ 0,\ 255)$; values within ±2σ of the mean fill the range and outliers saturate.
concepts.significance: Without it, raw ReLU activations with very different magnitudes would be mostly invisible or saturated in a single colormap.
concepts.example: A channel with mean 0.4 and std 0.2: value 0.8 → 64·2 + 128 = 256 → clipped to 255.
concepts.misconception: Brightness in figure 10.3 is relative within a channel. A bright tile in a deep layer does not mean a larger absolute activation than in layer 1.

concepts.name: Intermediate activation
concepts.definition: The output of a hidden Conv2D or MaxPooling2D layer for a given input.
concepts.intuition: A snapshot of the image's re-description at each depth.
concepts.technical: Shape (1, size, size, n_features), as the listing's callout states.
concepts.significance: Listing 10.6 renders all nine of them.
concepts.example: The last one, conv2d_15, is (1, 7, 7, 512): 32 grid rows of 16 tiny 7 × 7 tiles.
concepts.misconception: Pooling activations are also included, not only convolutions.

math.title: Per-channel display normalization
math.source_text: channel_image -= channel_image.mean(); channel_image /= channel_image.std(); channel_image *= 64; channel_image += 128; np.clip(channel_image, 0, 255).astype("uint8")

variables.meaning: Raw activation of the channel at row i, column j
Mean and (population) standard deviation of the channel over all S × S positions
Display value in [0, 255], cast to uint8

math.operations: Standardize, scale by 64, shift by 128, clip and convert to 8-bit integers. Skipped entirely if the channel sums to zero.
math.purpose: Bring every channel into the same visible range regardless of its raw scale.
math.interpretation: The mean maps to mid-gray level 128; one standard deviation corresponds to 64 levels, so the range [μ − 2σ, μ + 2σ] spans [0, 256] and anything beyond saturates.

math.source_text: n_cols = n_features // images_per_row; np.zeros(((size + 1) * n_cols - 1, images_per_row * (size + 1) - 1))

variables.meaning: `size`, the side of each channel image
Number of channels in the layer
Number of tile rows stacked vertically (despite the name)

math.operations: Each tile takes S pixels plus 1 separator pixel; the trailing separator is removed by the −1.
math.purpose: Allocate exactly enough space for all channels with 1-pixel gaps.
math.interpretation: The grid is always 16 tiles wide; its height grows with the number of channels.
math.intuition: Like laying out photos on a contact sheet with thin borders.
math.numerical_example: First layer: S = 178, 32 channels → n_cols = 2, grid 357 × 2863. Last layer: S = 7, 512 channels → n_cols = 32, grid 255 × 127.

code.title: Visualizing every channel in every intermediate activation
code.original_code:
images_per_row = 16
for layer_name, layer_activation in zip(layer_names, activations):
    n_features = layer_activation.shape[-1]
    size = layer_activation.shape[1]
    n_cols = n_features // images_per_row
    display_grid = np.zeros(
        ((size + 1) * n_cols - 1, images_per_row * (size + 1) - 1)
    )
    for col in range(n_cols):
        for row in range(images_per_row):
            channel_index = col * images_per_row + row
            channel_image = layer_activation[0, :, :, channel_index].copy()
            if channel_image.sum() != 0:
                channel_image -= channel_image.mean()
                channel_image /= channel_image.std()
                channel_image *= 64
                channel_image += 128
            channel_image = np.clip(channel_image, 0, 255).astype("uint8")
            display_grid[
                col * (size + 1) : (col + 1) * size + col,
                row * (size + 1) : (row + 1) * size + row,
            ] = channel_image
    scale = 1.0 / size
    plt.figure(
        figsize=(scale * display_grid.shape[1], scale * display_grid.shape[0])
    )
    plt.title(layer_name)
    plt.grid(False)
    plt.axis("off")
    plt.imshow(display_grid, aspect="auto", cmap="viridis")
code.what_it_does: For each of the nine layer activations, builds one image that tiles all its channels (16 per row) after normalizing each channel to [0, 255], and displays it titled with the layer name.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: iterates over the activations and the names of the corresponding layers (from listings 10.3/10.4).
Callout: the layer activation has shape (1, size, size, n_features). The last axis gives the channel count and axis 1 the spatial size (square maps).
Callout: prepares an empty grid for all channels. `n_cols` is the number of tile rows; each tile takes size+1 pixels including a 1-pixel separator.
Double loop over grid positions; `channel_index = col * 16 + row` fills the grid left to right, top to bottom.
Callout: a single channel (feature). `.copy()` avoids modifying `activations` in place with the following in-place operations.
Callout: normalizes channel values within [0, 255]; all-zero channels are kept at zero. Standardize, ×64, +128, then clip and cast to uint8.
Callout: places the channel matrix in the grid. Row slice `col*(size+1) : col*(size+1)+size` and the analogous column slice.
Figure size in inches is grid size divided by `size`, i.e. about 16 inches wide and `n_cols` inches tall, the same for every layer.
Callout: displays the grid for the layer, with title, no grid lines or axes, and viridis colormap; `aspect="auto"` lets the image fill the figure.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: `layer_names` (9 strings) and `activations` (9 arrays). Output: nine Matplotlib figures, together figure 10.3 (p.314).
code.algorithm: For each layer: allocate grid → for each channel: copy, normalize if non-zero, clip/cast, paste → display.
code.theory_link: Per-channel plotting follows from channels encoding relatively independent features (p.309). Blank tiles visualize sparsity in deeper layers (p.314).

parameters.name: images_per_row
parameters.role: Number of tiles per grid row (16). All channel counts here (32–512) are multiples of 16.
Display scale and offset: 1 std = 64 gray levels, mean = 128.

pitfalls: Variable naming is swapped relative to the usual convention: `col` indexes vertical tile rows and `row` indexes horizontal positions.
If n_features were not a multiple of 16, `//` would silently drop the last channels.
Note (not in the book): a constant but non-zero channel has std 0, so the division would produce NaN/inf; the guard only catches sums equal to zero.
Without `.copy()`, the in-place `-=`/`/=` would corrupt the stored activations.
Outside a notebook you may need `plt.show()` to see the figures.

deeper.title: Where each channel lands in the grid
deeper.body: For the first layer (size 178, 32 channels), `n_cols = 2`. Channel 5 has `col = 0, row = 5`, so it occupies rows 0–177 and columns 5·179 = 895 to 895+177 = 1072. Channel 21 has `col = 1, row = 5`, so it occupies rows 179–356 and the same columns. Row 178 and every 179th column remain 0 (the separators), which appear as thin dark lines in figure 10.3.

deeper.title: Why standardize instead of min–max scaling?
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): min–max scaling `(x - min)/(max - min) * 255` would let a single very bright pixel squeeze everything else into dark values. Standardization with clipping at about ±2σ is more robust to such outliers and gives tiles a consistent mid-gray background. The cost is that strong peaks saturate.

deeper.title: Why the book's channel may differ from yours
deeper.body: Two orchestras playing the same symphony seat their violinists in different chairs. The music (the function the network computes) is the same, but 'chair 6' holds a different player. Channel indices in a convnet are like those chairs.

misconceptions.correction: The book explicitly warns that learned filters aren't deterministic; your channel 5 may encode something else.

misconceptions.claim: Brighter tiles in deeper layers mean larger activations.
misconceptions.correction: Each tile is normalized separately, so brightness is relative within a channel. Only blank (all-zero) tiles are comparable in absolute terms.

misconceptions.correction: In the listing it is the number of tile rows stacked vertically; the grid always has 16 tiles horizontally.

takeaways: The sixth first-layer channel looks like a diagonal edge detector, but learned filters vary between runs.
Listing 10.6 renders all channels of all nine activations, 16 tiles per row with 1-pixel separators.
Each channel is standardized, mapped to mean 128 with 64 levels per std, clipped to [0, 255] and cast to uint8.
All-zero channels are left at zero, so blank tiles in figure 10.3 really are inactive filters.
Figure size scales with the grid so every layer's figure is about 16 inches wide.

questions.question: Why might your own channel 5 not look like a diagonal edge detector?
questions.answer: Because the filters a convolution layer learns are not deterministic; random initialization and stochastic training produce different filters in different orders.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly. Channel indices have no fixed meaning because filters can be permuted without changing the function.

questions.question: For the layer `max_pooling2d_7` with activation shape (1, 43, 43, 64), what are n_cols and the shape of display_grid?
A channel has mean 2 and standard deviation 0.5. What display value does a raw activation of 2.5 receive?
questions.explanation: (2.5 − 2)/0.5 = 1 standard deviation; 1·64 + 128 = 192. 128 would be the mean, 160 is half a std, and 255 would need ≥ about 2σ.

questions.question: Why does the listing check `channel_image.sum() != 0` before normalizing?
questions.answer: An all-zero channel has standard deviation 0, so dividing by it would produce NaN; the check keeps such channels at zero (shown as blank tiles).
questions.explanation: The callout says all-zero channels are kept at zero. With ReLU outputs, a zero sum means the filter did not fire anywhere.

questions.question: Which grid position (col, row) does channel_index 37 occupy, and which pixel rows does it span for a layer with size 87?
questions.explanation: From `channel_index = col * images_per_row + row` and the slice `col * (size + 1) : (col + 1) * size + col` = 176 : 263.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `.copy()` when extracting channel_image?
options: To convert the array to uint8
To avoid modifying the original activations with the in-place operations that follow
To move the array from GPU to CPU
questions.answer: To avoid modifying the original activations with the in-place operations that follow
questions.explanation: NumPy slicing returns a view; `-=`, `/=` etc. would write into `activations`. Casting happens later with astype, the arrays are already NumPy, and the batch axis is removed by the `[0, ...]` index.

questions.question: Could you rewrite listing 10.6 so it handles channel counts that are not multiples of 16? What would you change?
questions.answer: Use ceiling division for the number of tile rows and skip channel indices ≥ n_features.
questions.explanation: This checks that you understand how the grid size and channel indexing interact.
